questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Frame work?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Balangkas” = frame work. Origin: Tagalog balangkas “skeleton, framework”. Same idea: the bare bones of the building.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Nailers?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Pamakuan” = nailers. Origin: Tagalog pako “nail” with the pam- ... -an pattern, so “what you nail onto”.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Ceiling joist?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Kostilyahe” = ceiling joist. Origin: Spanish costilla “rib” (costillaje = ribbing). Ceiling joists are the closely spaced ribs of the ceiling.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Top chord is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Tahilan” = top chord. Native term; origin not confirmed. Memory hook: tahilan ~ tahi “to sew”; the top chord stitches the two roof slopes together at the peak.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Collar plate is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Sinturon” = collar plate. Origin: Spanish cinturón “belt”. A collar plate wraps and ties the frame like a belt.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Purlins is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Reostra” = purlins. Likely origin: Spanish riostra “brace, stay”, a member that stiffens the roof frame. I couldn't confirm it.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Pile is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Pilote” = pile. Origin: Spanish pilote “pile”, the same root as English “pile”.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Girder?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Guililian / Sepo / Kuling” = girder. Native/common terms for the main horizontal member of a house frame; origins not confirmed (Sepo may come from Spanish cepo “block, log”). Memory hook: guililian ~ gilid “side, edge”: the girder runs along the edges where beams rest. The same term is also used for: girt.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Abutment?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Tulay” = abutment. Origin: Tagalog tulay “bridge”. An abutment is the end support of a bridge.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Bottom chord?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Barakilan / Tirante” = bottom chord. Origin: tirante is Spanish for a tie, from tirar “to pull”. The bottom chord of a truss works in tension, pulling the two sides together.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Wall post?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Bagad” = wall post. Native Filipino term; origin not confirmed. Memory hook: bagad sounds like bakod “fence, enclosure”: the wall post is what a wall stands on.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Rafters?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Kilo” = rafters. Native term; origin not confirmed. Kilo is used for both the truss and the rafter. Memory hook: think of the whole roof frame as kilo. The same term is also used for: truss.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Post?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Halige / Poste” = post. Origin: poste is Spanish for “post”; halige is the Tagalog haligi “post, pillar”, the pillar of a house.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Queen post?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Prases / Sobre Pindulo” = queen post. Memory aid: Prases may come from English “braces” (unconfirmed). Sobre Pindulo means “beside/over the king post”: queen posts come as a pair next to the king post.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Column?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Kolumna, Haligue” = column. Origin: Spanish columna, the same word as English “column”. Haligue is a spelling of Tagalog haligi “post, pillar”.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Horizontal stud is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Pabalagbag / Trabe Anzo” = horizontal stud. Origin: trabe is Spanish for a beam, from Latin trabs. A horizontal stud is a small beam laid across the wall frame.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Truss is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Kilo” = truss. Native term; origin not confirmed. Kilo is used for both the truss and the rafter. Memory hook: think of the whole roof frame as kilo. The same term is also used for: rafters.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Brace (including diagonal brace) is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Pie de Gallo” = brace (including diagonal brace). Origin: Spanish pie de gallo “rooster's foot”. Memory aid: a diagonal brace splays out like a rooster's foot.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, King post / pendulum is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Pendulon / Pindulo” = king post / pendulum. Origin: Spanish péndulo and pendolón “pendulum”, the architect's word for a king post. It hangs from the ridge like a pendulum.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Vertical stud?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Pilarete” = vertical stud. Likely from Spanish pilar “pillar” + the diminutive -ete, so “little pillar”. A vertical stud is a small pillar in the wall frame.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Girt?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Sepo” = girt. Likely borrowed from Spanish cepo “block, log”, a heavy timber. Sepo is also listed for the girder, so girt and girder are close cousins. The same term is also used for: girder.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Jack rafter?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Sobre Kilo” = jack rafter. Origin: Spanish sobre “over, upon” + kilo (rafter). A jack rafter is the short kilo sitting over the main frame.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Joist?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Soleras / Suleras” = joist. Origin: Spanish solera, a base timber that other members rest on, related to suelo “floor, ground”. Suleras is a spelling variant of Soleras. The same term is also used for: floor joists.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Floor joists?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Soleras / Suleras” = floor joists. Origin: Spanish solera, a base timber that other members rest on, related to suelo “floor, ground”. Memory aid: floor joists are the soleras under your feet. The same term is also used for: joist.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Beam?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Biga” = beam. Origin: Spanish viga “beam”. Filipino spelling swaps v for b.
